1:
Whether the opening lament is over calamity or over wickedness is the first thing settled. Calvin reports that some refer it to the punishment already inflicted, the prophet surveying a disordered land, and answers that the following verse makes it plain he speaks of the people's wickedness instead; he therefore takes the two verses together. He also rejects a rendering he thinks too free, one that makes the prophet a man seeking summer fruit and burning with disappointed desire, on the ground that it cannot possibly be got out of the words. His own reading is that the land, which he says the prophet personifies throughout, is like a field or vineyard already stripped of all its fruit after harvest and vintage. He knows the alternative, that the gleanings left carelessly on the vines stand for a few just men remaining, and prefers the emptier picture as agreeing better with the rest of the passage. Keil and Delitzsch set the whole chapter in order before commenting, as a penitential prayer of the believing church answering the previous threatening, rising through belief in God's fidelity to confident hope, appending a prayer for renewed manifestations of grace, receiving the Lord's promise to renew the wonders of old, and closing with praise of his mercy.

Who is speaking, and when, is answered differently by each. Gill takes the complaint in the prophet's own name or in the name of the church of his time. Wesley makes the land itself the complainant, once well stored and now having few good in it. Henry considers the dating and reports that the description seems to some scarcely to agree with the reign under which the prophet worked, so that they take it as a prediction of a later and worse reign; he prefers an earlier reign, or the beginning of the reforming one before the reformation took effect, adding that even at its best, when the king had done what he could to purge out corruptions, much remained amiss. Clarke reads the prophet as the last man standing, seeming to be the only person on God's side and considering himself a solitary grape escaped from the general gathering.

The figure itself is worked at by three voices. Clarke reports that the word sometimes used for summer and summer fruit is here rendered late figs, and may be set against the early ripe fig of superior quality, so that the prophet desired to see distinguished and eminent piety and found only an imperfect or spurious godliness. Ellicott states the same comparison more simply, that as the early fig gathered in June is eagerly sought by the traveller so the prophet sought anxiously for a good man, and found the psalmist's experience, that the godly man ceases and the faithful fail. Wesley reads the vine as what the two kingdoms ought to have been, a fruitful vine full of clusters, so that just and compassionate and humble men are now only what is left after the vintage is gathered.
2: On the good man who has perished the voices agree on the sense of the word and differ on the sense of the perishing. Gill defines him as one who has received the grace of God and lives a godly life, and is particularly kind and merciful to those in distress; he is careful that the perishing means their bodily death and not the perishing of their graces or their comforts or their souls. Calvin gives the philology behind the same term, that it means kind, benevolent, merciful, actively good, and that the second word describes one proceeding in a straight course by the rule of the law without turning aside into any devious path. Keil and Delitzsch render the same complaint as the universal corruption which the church confesses in its prayer. On the hunting with a net, Ellicott derives the word from a verb meaning to shut up and notes that such a net served fisherman and fowler alike, so that men lay wait for one another as hunters for wild beasts. Calvin takes the same clause for perfidy and the preceding one for a thirst after blood, and adds the rhetorical observation that the manner adopted here is more emphatic than if God had pronounced the words in his own name, since the land is introduced accusing its own children, confessing its guilt, and anticipating God's judgment by acknowledging itself contaminated by its own inhabitants so that nothing pure remained in it. Gill also marks the transition, that what the prophet had delivered in figurative terms he now expresses in plain words, and understands the complaint of the land of Israel in particular, where such men had once been numerous and were now all dead and gone. Clarke sees a quite different picture and expounds it at length: an allusion to the ancient duel in which one combatant carried a casting net and tried to throw it over his opponent's head before finishing him with a short sword, while the other parried and, when the cast missed, pursued him about the field before the net could be set again; and he notes that a translator who missed the allusion rendered the clause that they hunt every man his brother for his destruction, though he put net in the margin.
3:
The oxymoron of doing evil well is handled four ways. Gill takes the adverb as strenuously and diligently, remarking that the wicked are generally more industrious in their evil than good men in their good, and reports an alternative reading the clause as doing evil instead of doing good, with the renderings of the Greek, Syriac and Targum. Clarke gives the same sense of earnestly and greedily and records a Latin rendering that avoids the difficulty by making them call the evil of their hands good. Ellicott states the literal sense and reports a modern Jewish translation, made under a chief rabbi's supervision, which sidesteps the oxymoron by rendering it as concerning the evil which their hands should amend, a version he judges to harmonise satisfactorily with the passage. Wesley says it means with all diligence.

The venality of the officers draws Clarke into his own country's history. He explains that the prince asks a bribe to forward claims and the judge a reward to decide for whoever gives most, whether the cause be good or bad, then observes that this was notoriously the case in England before the great charter, from which came the provision that justice shall not be sold to any man; and England, he adds, was not the only country where justice was put to sale. Wesley identifies the great man as the one at court who can do as he likes there and is bold to speak his unjust design plainly. On the closing clause Clarke takes it that they conjoin in doing evil in their several offices, and notes that the versions render the word variously, one giving simply that they do abominably; Ellicott renders it literally that they twist it and pervert justice.

The comparison of the best men to briers is agreed and briefly extended. Gill says they are good for nothing but burning, and Wesley that they are mischievous. Keil and Delitzsch put it that the best man resembles the thorn-bush, which only pricks and injures. Clarke adds what gives the figure its force, that such men are useless in themselves and cannot be touched without wounding whoever comes near them, the allusion being to the thick thorn hedges still frequent in that country.

The day of the watchmen is understood by all as the announced day of reckoning. Ellicott glosses it as the time the prophets had foreseen and warned of, and quotes another prophet on watchmen set over a people who refused to hearken. Wesley calls it the day in which the alarm is sounded, coming surely and unavoidably. Clarke makes it the day of vengeance and turns the earlier image against them, that now there shall be no more wrapping up but all unfolded, so every man will wish he were other than he is found to be and be judged for what he is.

The warning against trusting a friend is where the chapter becomes personal. Gill fences it about: the words are not meant to lessen the value of friendship, nor discourage cultivating it, nor weaken confidence in a real friend, one of the great blessings of life, but to show how far the age had degenerated, men who pretended friendship being so universally faithless that no dependence could be had on them. Clarke gives instead a note he wrote on the passage a quarter of a century before and now reprints: that several whom he had delighted to call friends deceived him, that had he followed certain guides he should have gone to perdition, and that his wife alone never deceived him; after twenty-seven years, he adds, he finds no cause to alter it. Calvin reads the same verses as iniquity arrived at its highest point, faithfulness gone and humanity with it, the son failing in his duty to his father and the daughter-in-law to her mother-in-law, so no mutual love or concord remained.
7:
The turn from complaint to hope is marked by everyone, and the reason given for it is the same in each mouth. Wesley says the therefore rests on the perfidy just described, and reads the looking as the act of one set in a watchtower who observes diligently all that stirs. Clarke puts it as a conclusion from the state of things, that because matters are so he will trust the more firmly, wait the more patiently, and expect the more confidently to be saved. Ellicott gives the same movement its landscape, that because of all this gloom settled on the earth he will for his part lift his eyes to the everlasting hills on which the light of God's presence rests. Henry draws the general rule: the prophet had complained that no confidence could be put in friends on earth, and this drives him to his God, so that the less reason we have to delight in any creature the more reason we have to delight in God. Gill expands the looking into an inventory, prayer and holy freedom and confidence and expectation, and reports that the Targum interprets the clause of the Word of the Lord, which he takes for the Son of God, to be looked to in all his offices and for all things.

The address to the enemy raises the question who is meant, and the answers run from the historical to the spiritual. Clarke identifies the speakers as the captive Israelites and the enemy as the Assyrians and Chaldeans, the fall as their idolatry and captivity, the darkness as the calamities suffered in it, and the rising as their restoration. Ellicott makes a grammatical point the others miss, that the Hebrew word is strictly a female enemy used of enemies collectively, and proposes two cities named together in a psalm of exile; their fall, he adds, was final, whereas Jerusalem would rise again. Gill allows the literal identification and extends it to the great enemy of mankind, who takes pleasure in drawing the people of God into snares, and to the men of the world who watch for the halting of the saints, adding that the turn of their enemies to be afflicted will come. Calvin reads the verse as the church repelling a temptation, since in adversity there is less bitterness in the evil itself than in the mockery of the wicked, reproach being sharper to noble minds than death; and he calls the tactic the devil's usual artifice, that seeing us stand firm he suborns the wicked and sharpens their tongues to wound us with slanders.

Clarke alone turns the verse on his own contemporaries. He states the principle first, that to rejoice over the fall or the miseries of any man betrays a malignant spirit, and then gives the instances he has known: people professing a pure and Christian creed having become unfaithful and fallen into sin, their opponents, who held a creed he calls impure and unchristian, exulted openly that this was what they had wanted, and showed their malignity further by giving such accounts all possible publicity and circulation. He judges that in God's sight this exultation may have been worse than the fall exulted in, since what pleased them was that the fallen man held a creed different from their own; and he closes by observing that the fallen rose again while those who jeered at holiness continued in the gall of bitterness. Henry keeps the verses within the covenant relation, the indignation just because sin provoked it, and we must own as much under divine rebukes, so as to justify God and answer his end by repenting and breaking off from the sin. Keil and Delitzsch supply the verses and mark the movement, the church rising through belief in the fidelity of God to the confident hope that its enemies shall not triumph over it.
9:
The bearing of the indignation is treated as the mark of genuine repentance, and Calvin analyses it most closely. He says the church encourages herself to patience by two arguments, first setting her sins before her and so humbling herself before a judge she acknowledges to be just, and then embracing the hope of forgiveness, from which confidence of deliverance arises; on these two supports she sustains herself so as not to fail. He observes that the word for the indignation means a stormy anger that raises tempests, which is what the calamities were, and then draws the general rule: whoever is seriously touched with a conviction of God's judgment is by that very fact prepared to exercise patience, so that when men clamour against God or murmur it is certain they have not yet been made sensible of their sins. He is careful to distinguish confession from repentance, allowing that many feel guilty while still struggling against God and blaspheming under his chastisement, and citing two who owned that they had sinned without repenting at all, one confessing freely and the other only under compulsion. Ellicott makes the same point from a different case, the king who when his sin was brought home to him chose to fall into the hand of the Lord rather than the hand of man, and says this is the temper of all penitents under chastisement. Clarke identifies the speakers as the penitent captives acknowledging their sins, and adds a warning to the slanderers of the preceding verse, that woe is theirs when God undertakes to plead for the fallen who have returned to him with deep compunction. Gill notes only what the Targum prefixes to the words, and Wesley glosses the pleading as God taking up the church's cause against the enemy who now pleads his own against her, and the righteousness as the truth and riches of his promised salvation.

Who the enemy is that shall see it draws out both the historical and the ecclesiastical readings. Clarke takes it particularly of Babylon and then reports its end with unusual concreteness: the taking of the city by the Persians and its total ruin, its walls made of brick kneaded with straw and baked in the sun dissolving under the wet until no vestige of the city remains, except a few bricks dug out from under the rubbish, several pieces of which he says lie before him as he writes and show the perishing materials of which the head of that proud empire was built. Ellicott keeps to the taunt rather than the masonry, that the enemy who had jeered at the powerlessness of Israel's God should be trodden down when the deliverance came, and instances the invader who asked contemptuously whether the Lord could deliver the city out of his hand. Gill reports that some Jewish authorities read the enemy as Rome, meaning by that the Christians as against themselves, and turns the identification round, suggesting that it would not be amiss to understand papal Rome as against the church of God, since the antichristian party will see the slain witnesses rise; he adds that the verse may be applied to any age of the church and to any particular saints raised out of darkness in the sight of their enemies. Calvin notices the figure that governs the whole passage, that the enemies are described under the character of an envious woman just as the church is elsewhere compared to a woman, and remarks that this manner of speaking is common in Scripture. Keil and Delitzsch give the verses and mark their place, the church looking for the Lord to procure it justice and deeply humble the foe.
11:
Whom the promise about the rebuilt walls addresses is disputed before anything else can be settled. Gill reports two readings that make it an address to the enemy, either the Chaldeans whose capital was demolished and would be long in rebuilding, or a later enemy planning to build with the spoils of Israel, and rejects both; his own view is that the prophet comforts the church, since a day would come when the walls and temple, lying in ruins through the captivity, would be rebuilt, fulfilled under the two leaders of the return. Clarke reaches the same conclusion by stating what he cannot think, that the verse threatens Jerusalem rather than promising, since God had purposed the return. On the decree that is to be far removed the answers diverge. Wesley identifies it as the royal order forbidding the rebuilding, and its removal as its abolition. Ellicott says the word means something definite, an appointed law or statute, and reports two interpretations, that the law of separation between Jew and Gentile is removed, or that God's decree concerned distant nations who should press into his kingdom; he prefers the second as agreeing with the effect of the decree, which brought people to Jerusalem from the ends of the world.

The gathering from the four quarters produces three renderings and a wide disagreement about the geography. Gill again rejects the reading that makes the verse an address to the enemy, and takes it as a continued address to the church, the Jews with proselyted Gentiles coming from all parts to rebuild the city, and multitudes of nations flocking to the church of Christ. Clarke sets two translations side by side, one bringing them from Assyria and the fenced cities and from Egypt to the river, the other from Assyria to Egypt and thence to the Euphrates and from sea to sea and mountain to mountain; he prefers the second as giving an easy sense, since on the other nobody can tell where to find the fortified cities, and takes it as fulfilled when the nation was extended under the later dynasty. Ellicott translates it impersonally, that they shall come from Assyria and the cities of Egypt and thence to the river and from sea to sea and mountain to mountain, reading it as people coming from all parts of the earth; he compares another prophet's vision of Assyria and Egypt and Israel blessed together, and says the Christian reader can hardly refrain from discerning here the assembly of the nations at Pentecost. Wesley keeps it national, the returning Jews coming from the fortified cities where they were kept for servile work and from all parts of their captivity. Calvin admits obscurity in the words, which has led interpreters to supply different terms, and reports the proposal that one is a proper name giving from Mount Hor, though the prophet's meaning seems to him not doubtful.

The desolation that follows the promise is felt as a difficulty and handled in four ways. Ellicott states it as an emotional turn, bitterness still in the cup, the vision of the land's near desolation rising amid triumphant expectation. Clarke removes the difficulty by the tense, arguing the verb should be past, that the land had been desolate during the captivity, which was the fruit of the evil doings of those who dwelt there. Wesley leaves the order alone and measures the interval, the promises of restitution not taking place until more than two hundred years after. Gill takes the desolation as future and distributes it over three visitations, the northern kingdom wasted by one empire, the southern by another, and the land desolate a third time by the Romans; and he explains why the warning stands where it does, partly to prevent wicked men promising themselves impunity, partly to prevent good men despairing when it came. Keil and Delitzsch supply the verses plainly.
14:
Who prays and who is asked to feed is answered in three ways. Gill lays out the possibilities: the words may be the Father's to the Son as the great Shepherd; or the Son's to his ministers, to feed the sheep committed to their charge with sound doctrine; or, as Gill prefers, the prophet's own prayer that God would take care of his people in their captivity, guiding and protecting them as a shepherd governs his flock. Wesley takes the first, that Christ directs his officers so. Henry takes the third and draws a rule, that when God is about to deliver his people he stirs up their friends to pray, so that when we see him coming towards us in mercy we must meet him by prayer; and this prophetic prayer amounts to a promise, since what God directed his prophet to ask he designed to give. Calvin argues the same point from the sequence: there is more force in the passage than if it had simply been said that God would deliver, because the prophet interposed entreaty first, from which the faithful are reminded that they must be instant in prayer if they desire to be preserved.

The rod itself is corrected by two voices. Clarke says the word most certainly means the shepherd's crook, as the mention of a flock immediately after shows, and denies flatly that any rod of correction or affliction is intended or that the word can mean such a thing. Ellicott renders it the same way and turns to the people's condition, either dwelling alone among the idolaters of Babylon, among them but not of them, or living as a nation mysteriously apart after the return. Wesley notes the allusion to the custom of shepherds guiding sheep with a pastoral staff, and reads the dwelling in the wood as the solitary and endangered state of the captives. Henry develops the picture into an allegory of the exile, the people a peculiar flock dwelling alone and not reckoned among the nations, desolate in the land of their captivity like sheep in a forest, in danger of being made a prey to its beasts, scattered on the mountains as sheep having no shepherd.

The three place-names are taken as pasture by all who mention them. Clarke says the first is very fruitful in vines and the other two proverbially fruitful in pasturage. Wesley calls them all fruitful and well inhabited. Ellicott places the flock either on the fruitful mountain range or in the rich pasture land east of the Jordan, and then does something none of the others do, citing a contemporary book on that region which had lately brought its extraordinary fertility into prominence and predicted its future prosperity in glowing colours.

The answer that follows is agreed to be an answer, and its measure is the exodus. Gill states it as an assurance that a deliverance as great and as wonderful would be wrought as when Israel was brought out with a mighty hand, attended by the plagues and the passage of the sea and the destruction of the pursuers. Clarke says the same briefly, that God will protect and save and work miracles in their restoration such as he wrought for their fathers. Ellicott observes that the promise graciously recalls the earlier interposition and declares it shall be repeated. Calvin sharpens the relation between prayer and answer: the prophet had asked only that God would feed them and do kind things for them, and God replies that he will show them marvellous things and outdo their hopes and expectations, so that the deliverance from Babylon is to be a work of wonder and of grace. Keil and Delitzsch mark the same exchange structurally, the prayer for a renewal of the former manifestations of grace answered by the Lord's promise to renew for his people the wonders of the olden time.
16:
What the nations are confounded at is the strength they had trusted. Gill takes them first as the Babylonians ashamed of the power they had boasted of and unable to hold their captives any longer, then extends the verse to the confusion of the Gentile world at the spread of the gospel and the abolition of paganism, and reports a Jewish commentator who refers it instead to the nations gathered against Jerusalem in the latter day. Clarke declines to choose among the historical applications and says that whether the verses be referred to the return from captivity or to the later prosperity under the Maccabees, they may be understood as ultimately applying to a final restoration under the gospel. Calvin makes the verse an answer to a particular anxiety, as though the prophet said that he knows what makes them fearful, since many enemies are intent on their ruin and are ready to resist fiercely whenever help appears; the point is that however strongly armed the unbelieving think themselves, and whatever obstacles they hold in reserve, the whole will be in vain, God proving that the strength of men is mere nothing. He also glosses the clause about laying the hand on the mouth as meaning that they shall not dare to boast hereafter, the Hebrew phrase signifying to be silent.

The licking of the dust is explained twice from natural history and twice from court ceremonial. Ellicott hears in it the doom pronounced on the serpent and applies it to the determined enemies of the Lord and his people. Gill gives the same reference and then adds the physical detail, that a creature going on its belly cannot but take up dust along with its food, before turning to the other explanation: the allusion, he thinks, is to the manner of the eastern nations in complimenting their kings, bowing so low that they take the dust into their mouths, and he cites two reports of the practice, one that the Persians kiss the pavement the king treads before speaking to him. Calvin will not have the ceremonial reading at all and keeps the image simple, that to lick the dust is nothing else but to lie prostrate on the earth, so that enemies who had proudly exalted themselves shall be low and creeping like serpents. Wesley combines the two, a submissive and servile testimony of subjection.

The moving out of the holes is where Calvin does his philology. He notes that the verb can mean to raise an uproar or to move oneself, and prefers the second here, so that the enemies come forth from their enclosures; the noun he derives from a root meaning to close up and renders lurking-places rather than fortresses, though he grants that in a psalm the same word is applied to citadels, where men trembled from their strongholds because the fame of a king had broken their boldness. Because the prophet is speaking of worms, he keeps the humbler sense. Wesley takes the opposite view of the same word and renders it their strongholds and fastnesses, and reads the clause that follows as meaning that the name of the Jews shall be terrible to their enemies. Gill describes the whole condition as the low and abject and cursed estate of the seed of the serpent, forced to yield subjection and to pretend the profoundest respect.
18:
The closing question is understood by everyone as a challenge, and the ground of the challenge is what distinguishes the treatments. Gill takes it as a denial that there is any god besides, none so great for the perfections of his nature or the works of his hands, and especially for pardoning grace. Clarke reads it as a challenge to idol-worshippers and to those who take false views of the true God, and enumerates the characters that follow as five answers: that he pardons iniquity, the prerogative of God alone; that he passes by transgression, healing backsliding and restoring the fallen; that he does not retain anger for ever; that he delights in mercy, judgment being his strange work, so nothing pleases him better than an opportunity to spare a returning sinner; and that being such a God he turns again and casts sins into the sea. Ellicott observes that the prophet concludes with an allusion to the meaning of his own name, and claims that the gracious character here ascribed to God is unparalleled in the Bible among human utterances, being his response to the words God spoke of himself to Moses, the promise then made being here extended to the Gentiles.

Calvin takes the comparison as an argument rather than an exclamation, and answers an objection to it. He grants that the words do not mean there are other gods, and that a comparison strictly taken would be improper; the point is that the true God may be distinguished from every idol by this one circumstance, that he graciously forgives his people's sins and bears their infirmities. He then anticipates the reply that every nation thought its gods ready to pardon, which is why they had sacrifices and expiations, no nation being so barbarous as not to own itself guilty; and answers that they prayed with no sure confidence, holding the principle that the gods would be propitious to humble petitioners while possessing no certain promise. The proof, therefore, is not that the God of Israel forgives, but that having once received the children of Abraham into favour he kept his covenant inviolably though their sins had a thousand times stood in the way, his goodness surmounting all their wickedness.

The turning again is read as a change in appearance rather than in God. Gill is careful about it: the anger is not opposite to love but a displeasure at sin rather than at the persons of his people, so that properly it is not in God at all but rather in appearance than reality, God showing himself as if angry, withdrawing his presence, and returning when they are brought to a sense of sin. He also notices the manner of the passage, the prophet dwelling on this article of grace and heaping up words for it, as if unable to say too much. Calvin makes the same accumulation a lesson in application. He says the prophet prescribes a form of glorying, and that it avails little to understand something in general about God's mercy or to preach free remission at large without coming to the application; each of the faithful must conclude that God is merciful for his own sake as soon as he is called upon, and that since he forgives the remnant of his heritage because he is by nature inclined to mercy, he will be merciful to us. Unless that conclusion is laid hold of, he says, whatever we have heard or said about God's goodness will vanish away, and he calls this the true logic of religion. On the casting of the sins into the sea, Clarke records that five manuscripts and four ancient versions read our sins rather than their sins, and glosses the promise as an eternal oblivion from which they never come into sight again, like a stone dropped into the depths. Keil and Delitzsch supply the closing verses plainly.
20:
The closing verse is read by all as the ground on which the whole preceding hymn rests, and Calvin states the principle behind that reading. The faithful, he says, do not learn by their own understanding what sort of being God is but embrace the mercy he offers in his word; unless God speaks we can form no idea of his grace but an uncertain and vanishing one, whereas when he declares he will be merciful every doubt is removed. He puts the confession into their mouths accordingly, that they invent nothing out of their own minds but receive what God has testified, and, relying on his favour, are persuaded of a gratuitous pardon although in many respects guilty. He then notices the two terms by which the covenant is characterised here, truth and mercy, and observes that in order of cause the mercy comes first, since God is not induced to it by anything outside himself. Gill takes the same verse simply, that the promise made to the patriarch will be faithfully performed to his posterity, natural and spiritual, and especially to those who are Israelites indeed. Keil and Delitzsch give the verse without comment, having already marked the close of the chapter as the prophet's praise of the mercy and grace of the Lord.

Clarke and Ellicott both find the same later echo. Ellicott says the closing words are gloriously taken up some centuries afterwards in the song of the priest who spoke of God performing the mercy promised to the fathers and remembering his holy covenant. Clarke identifies the same passage and argues the identification, that the prophet's words were quoted as fulfilled in the incarnation by a man under the full influence of the Spirit, and he spells out what he takes the oath to have been, that in the patriarch's seed all the families of the earth should be blessed, the Messiah coming through the named line to be a light to the Gentiles and the glory of Israel. He adds that the promise was signally fulfilled in one sent to bless by turning every one from his iniquities, delivered for our offences and raised for our justification, with repentance and remission preached in his name to all nations and the proclamation made first at Jerusalem.

Clarke then quotes the Chaldee paraphrase of the verse at length, which he praises for spirit and propriety: that God will give the truth to Jacob as he promised him by oath at a named place, and the mercy to Abraham and his seed as he swore amidst the divisions, that he will be mindful of them on account of the binding of Isaac upon the altar, and will do the good promised to the fathers from the most ancient days. He explains that the phrase about the divisions refers to the covenant made when the pieces were divided. He closes the chapter with an exclamation rather than a comment, returning to the question that opened the hymn and declaring that hell is speechless and earth dumb before it, that the mighty God and Saviour pardons iniquity and transgression and sin and saves to the uttermost all who come to God through him, and he turns from the text to address his reader directly, bidding him lay this to heart.
